source.title: Feature Lottery? A Bifurcation Theory of Concept Emergence

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests modular-arithmetic delayed generalization with a GMM probe and representation-geometry measures, rather than reproducing the original study’s measurements alone.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own grokking experiments and a weight-decay sweep. Rows cover delayed test-accuracy transition timing, the relation to training fraction and weight decay, the NC1 trajectory, and the early β/βc indicator. The CIFAR and SAE results are not rows for these versions because they do not test delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data. Cited results about the Fourier circuit are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study trains the Nanda et al. modular-addition transformer and reports chance-to-1 test-accuracy jumps long after memorization (Table 2 'Memo' column, about 250 steps). It compares 30% vs 50% train fractions and sweeps weight decay over seven levels with 3 seeds each. These results bear directly on V1 and partly on V5. Its own continuous measures (GMM log(β/βc), NC1) are tracked through the plateau and bear on V2's progress-measure part. The measures are new rather than the originals', so it is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors read grokking as a fast β=βc crossing (about 40 steps) followed by a dissipation-controlled metastable plateau and an escape. Escape time falls as a power law in weight decay, with no escape at WD=0. They claim the indicator plus weight-decay strength forecasts whether and roughly when grokking happens. The grokking result is one part of a broader bifurcation and SAE 'feature lottery' paper.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a modular-addition transformer setup following Nanda et al., with an attached joint-detached GMM probe and NC1 representation measurements to analyze the transition. It does not focus solely on the original train/test-accuracy measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Escape time changes with weight decay and training fraction; the paper also reports dependence on modulus p. Kprobe changes the late magnitude of log(β/βc), while the reported crossing and grokking steps remain invariant across Kprobe = 2, 5, 10, 20, 50.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-decay escape times fit a power law (ΔAIC +19.3 over a Kramers exponential form), which the authors read as drift-dominated rather than activated escape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay scales as a power law in weight-decay strength (drift-dominated escape).

record.problems: The training-fraction comparison uses only 30% and 50%. Grokking results generally use n = 3 seeds; the indicator diagnostic’s early forecast is illustrated on the canonical run. The no-weight-decay control is observed only within a finite horizon. Circuit-level evidence for Fourier computation or removal of memorizing components is not provided.

untested.parts: Only two train fractions (0.3, 0.5) and only modular addition; no other algorithmic tasks.
No Fourier circuit, no circuit-level progress measures, and no removal of memorizing components.
No delayed-generalization result on non-algorithmic data; the CIFAR/SAE experiments are not grokking tests. No initialization-scale manipulation.
Circuit efficiency, critical dataset size and ungrokking are not tested; only the effect of weight decay on escape time.
Optimizer and numerical-precision artifacts are not examined.

missing.what: Table 2 'Memo' column: memorization steps per configuration (253±6, 297±49, 263±2, 242±52, 273±8), which quantify training-accuracy saturation for the delay.
Act 1 crossing step per configuration (37, 39, 36, 54, 36), including the WD=0 non-grokking control, showing the indicator is not specific to runs that grok.
Power-law fit τesc ∝ WD^-1.23 with fitted vs observed values.

record.verdict_notes: The record's claim that training-accuracy saturation is unquantified is wrong: Table 2 has a Memo column. The Kprobe rows are method-robustness checks and should not count as V2 evidence. The reader's V2 'supports' overstated the result: NC1 is flat through the plateau, and the indicator crosses even in the WD=0 control.

versions.untested_parts: Training-accuracy saturation is not explicitly quantified in the text. The smaller-training-set comparison uses only the 30% and 50% train fractions.
The paper does not identify or causally trace a Fourier generalization circuit, or show memorizing components being removed. Its progress measures are the GMM indicator and NC1.
The paper tests weight-decay effects on escape timing, but does not measure whether weight decay selects a more efficient circuit or establish a critical dataset size and ungrokking threshold.

rows.subject: 1-layer transformer (dmodel = 128, 4 heads, dmlp = 512)
rows.operation_detail: Track the GMM probe’s log(β/βc) during modular-addition training.
rows.baseline: Test accuracy has not yet provided a transition signal

rows.note: This is the paper’s early-warning progress measure, not a direct measure of the Fourier circuit.
rows.check: log(β/βc) crosses zero at about step 36–40 in every configuration, including the WD=0 control that never groks (Table 2). It marks eligibility but does not by itself anticipate whether or when the jump occurs; timing needs weight decay as an extra input.

relationships.reason: Memorization at about 250–300 steps, then a chance-to-1 jump thousands of steps later in 3/3 seeds. The 30% train fraction groks about 7× later than 50% (R1, R2, R3, R5–R9).
relationships.display_finding: All three seeds memorized around steps 250–300 before test accuracy jumped from chance to 100% thousands of steps later, with 30% training data grokking about seven times later than 50%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R1–R3 and R5–R9 report delayed generalization; Table 2 establishes early memorization and later grokking, with the smaller training fraction grokking later.

relationships.reason: Without weight decay, test accuracy stays at about 0.01 in 0/3 seeds despite memorization (R4); escape depends on weight decay.
relationships.display_finding: None of the three seeds generalized within 50,000 steps, with test accuracy remaining around 1% despite memorization.

relationships.display_finding: The GMM indicator became positive at about 40 steps even without grokking, while NC1 stayed flat until collapsing alongside the jump.

relationships.reason: Escape time decreases monotonically with weight decay, from 147k to 8.9k steps (about WD^-1.23), with no escape at WD=0. This is consistent with a low-norm bias driving generalization; the efficiency mechanism itself is untested (R4–R9).
relationships.display_finding: Escape time decreased monotonically from 147,000 to 8,900 steps as weight decay increased, scaling approximately as weight decay to the power −1.23; zero decay produced no escape.
